pages.text: How Computers Work

image.note: Cover: a child surrounded by a phone, tablet and laptop

pages.text: Contents. Just On and Off / The Brain of the Computer / Memory / Talking to the Computer / Following Instructions / The Machine We Made.

It is in your hand, on your desk, in your pocket, and all around your home. It plays your games, shows your videos, answers your questions, and never seems to tire. It can do millions of things, yet, deep down, it truly understands only two: on, and off. This is the story of the computer, the cleverest machine we have ever built, and how it really works.

image.note: Computers all around a child: phone, tablet, laptop

pages.text: Computers are everywhere now, and most of them do not even look like computers. There is one in a phone, and a tablet, and a game console, and even inside cars and washing machines. They seem almost like magic. But there is no magic in them at all, only a few simple ideas, done incredibly fast.

Here is the strangest secret of computers. Deep down, a computer cannot count to ten, or read a word, or see a picture. Underneath everything, it knows only two things: on, and off. Like a light switch, each tiny part inside it is either on, or off, and nothing in between.

image.note: A single switch, on and off

pages.text: How can a machine that knows only on and off do so much? By using millions of tiny switches together, and by agreeing that patterns of on and off can stand for other things. On and off can stand for numbers. Numbers can stand for letters. Letters can stand for words. Step by step, on and off can become anything at all.

image.note: Patterns of on and off becoming numbers, then letters

pages.text: This is called binary: a way of writing everything using just two signs, on and off, or one and zero. Every word you read on a screen, every colour in every picture, every note in every song, is really just a long, long pattern of ones and zeros, far too fast and too many for us to see.

image.note: A picture made of countless ones and zeros

pages.text: At the heart of every computer is its brain, called the processor. It is a tiny chip, smaller than a stamp, and its one great skill is this: it can do very simple sums, like adding and comparing numbers, but it can do them at a speed almost impossible to imagine.

image.note: The tiny processor chip at the computer's heart

pages.text: How fast? A modern processor can do billions of tiny steps every single second. Billions. In the time it takes you to blink, it has done more sums than you could do in many lifetimes. It is not clever the way you are clever. It is simple, and obedient, and unbelievably, dizzyingly fast.

image.note: The processor working at incredible speed

pages.text: A computer must also remember things: your game, your photos, the words you are typing this very second. So every computer has memory, where it stores information as those same patterns of on and off, ready to be used again.

image.note: Information stored in the computer's memory

pages.text: There are two kinds of memory. One holds what the computer is working on right now, and forgets it the moment you switch off, like a thought held in your head for a moment. The other stores things for keeps, your photos and your games, safe even when the power is gone, like words written down in a book.

For a computer to be useful, you must be able to tell it things, and it must be able to show you things back. The parts you use to put information in, a keyboard, a mouse, a touchscreen, a microphone, are called input. You are putting information into the machine.

The parts that give information back to you, the screen that shows the picture, the speaker that makes the sound, are called output. Information coming out. Every time you tap a screen and watch it answer, you are using input and output, talking with a machine that listens and replies.

But a computer, for all its speed, cannot decide anything for itself. It only ever does exactly what it is told, step by step, in the right order. A list of instructions for a computer is called a program, and writing one is called coding.

image.note: A program shown as a clear list of instructions

pages.text: This is the golden rule of computers, and every coder learns it first: the computer does precisely what you tell it, not what you meant. If a program goes wrong, the computer is not being silly. It is following your instructions perfectly, and the mistake, somewhere, is yours to find. That is why coders must be so careful, and so clear.

Everything a computer does, every game, every app, every website, is really a program: a huge, careful list of simple instructions, followed at tremendous speed. People write these programs, and the computer, obedient and fast, carries them out exactly, millions of steps a second.

image.note: People writing the programs that run the world

pages.text: So now you know the secret of the machine in your hand. It knows only on and off. It stores and reads them as patterns. Its tiny brain does simple sums at dizzying speed. You talk to it through input, and it answers through output. And all of it follows programs, written by people, step by careful step.

image.note: The whole computer explained in one picture

pages.text: There is no magic in a computer, only clever ideas, done fast, and instructions, followed exactly. And the most wonderful part is this: people build them, and people tell them what to do. Perhaps, one day, you will write the programs that machines like these will follow. The cleverest machine we have ever made is waiting for your instructions.

image.note: A child at a computer, ready to code

pages.text: Words to know. Binary: writing everything with just two signs, on and off. Processor: the computer's brain, which does simple sums very fast. Memory: where a computer stores information. Input: information going into a computer. Output: information coming out. Program: a list of instructions a computer follows.

image.note: Labelled diagram of a computer's parts

pages.text: Computers run our games, our phones, and much of our modern world, yet they only ever do what people tell them. Now you know how. What might you build, or fix, or dream up, with a machine this fast and this obedient at your command?

image.note: A child imagining what to build with computers
